record_identity.title: One participant's authority treated as sufficient for another participant's capture or processing

summary: A multi-party authority failure in which a participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, or tool user introduces an AI capture, transcription, recording, analysis, or comparable processing system and the system treats that person's authority, account status, invitation, or tool use as sufficient authority over another participant's identifiable contribution. The failure is not that multi-party capture exists; many meeting, classroom, conference, clinical, workplace, and service contexts legitimately require capture of other participants. The failure is the absence of an independently adequate authority, notice, consent, legal basis, or other governance condition for the affected participant and the specific processing at issue.
why_it_matters_to_CAM: Multi-human systems require participant-aware authority rather than a single-user permission model. One person's choice to use an AI notetaker may legitimately establish the tool's presence in a workflow while remaining insufficient to settle the rights and authority state of every other person captured. The required diligence rises with vulnerability and consequence, including where minors, biometric voice or image data, confidential professional material, health information, protected classes, or other sensitive contexts are involved. Public availability or attendance can alter the authority analysis but should not operate as an automatic permission bit for every form of capture or processing.
evidence_confidence: incident-database cluster with underlying litigation allegations; mechanism admitted as recurring governance risk, liability not adjudicated

source_records.source_title: Incident 1650: Otter.ai Notetaker Allegedly Recorded Meeting Conversations Without Participants' Informed Consent and Used Data for AI Training
source_records.model_or_algorithm: AI speech-to-text and meeting transcription system
source_records.deployment_context: Virtual workplace meetings involving multiple participants where an AI notetaker was introduced into Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, or comparable meeting environments.
source_records.source_context: AIID records allegations that Otter.ai captured private meeting conversations without every participant's informed consent. The same incident record also alleges downstream use for AI training; FM-0073 relies only on the participant-authority and capture aspect, while secondary-use training authority is separated into FM-0074.
source_records.relevance_note: Supports the recurring mechanism that one participant's use of a meeting tool can affect non-user participants whose authority state is not necessarily established by the tool user's own account or consent.

source_records.source_title: Incident 1652: Granola AI Notetaker Allegedly Captured and Transcribed Florida Meeting Participant Without Notice or Consent
source_records.model_or_algorithm: AI meeting notetaker and transcription system
source_records.deployment_context: Virtual meeting in which another participant used the AI notetaker and a non-user participant's speech was allegedly captured and transcribed without notice or consent.
source_records.source_context: AIID records the allegation that a Florida meeting participant was captured and transcribed after another participant used Granola. The record also reports allegations concerning model-improvement use and a weaker opt-out position for non-users; FM-0073 relies on the capture/participant-authority aspect, while FM-0074 owns the downstream secondary-use mechanism.
source_records.relevance_note: Strongly illustrates the core FM: the affected participant is not the person who invoked the tool, yet their identifiable contribution is processed because another participant brought the service into the interaction.

contextual_relations.rationale: FM-0073 concerns whether authority from one participant or organiser validly extends to another person's capture or processing. FM-0074 concerns whether an authorised primary use of data validly extends to a materially different secondary purpose such as model training. Either can occur without the other.
FM-0056 concerns technical access or reachability being mistaken for authority. FM-0073 instead concerns transposition of one human participant's authority onto another affected human participant.

failure_mode_definition: A failure mode in which authority held or asserted by one participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, or tool user to introduce or operate an AI capture, transcription, recording, analysis, biometric-processing, or comparable system is treated as sufficient authority over another affected participant's identifiable contribution without independently establishing the authority, notice, consent, legal basis, representative authority, or other governance condition required for that participant and processing context. The failure does not prohibit multi-party capture. It requires participant-aware authority resolution proportionate to the context, the type of processing, the sensitivity of the contribution, and the rights or vulnerabilities of the people affected.
failure_threshold: The threshold is met when: (1) a multi-party interaction contains identifiable contributions from more than one human; (2) one participant, organiser, host, account holder, deployer, or tool user introduces or operates an AI system that captures or materially processes the interaction; (3) another participant's identifiable speech, image, biometric representation, text, behaviour, or contribution is captured or materially processed; (4) the system or deployer relies on the invoking participant's authority, account status, invitation, or tool use as sufficient authority for the affected participant; and (5) the authority state applicable to that participant has not been independently established to the level required for the context and use. Public accessibility, attendance, or visibility may be relevant to the authority assessment but does not by itself settle every downstream capture or processing question. Multi-party presence alone is not a failure, and a valid basis that independently covers the affected participant and use defeats the threshold.

failure_classification.persistence: can persist across repeated meetings, standing bots, workplace integrations, classrooms, conferences, service calls, and institutional deployments

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The core mechanism is transposition of authority from one human participant or organiser to another affected participant whose contribution requires an independently adequate authority determination.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Authority tied to one principal is carried into another principal's contribution without fresh validation.
